title: One leg in the community, one leg in the health system: A qualitative study of stakeholder perspectives on South Africa's community health worker programme and lessons for Belgium
content:
by Laura Vroonen, Caroline Masquillier, Hilde Bastiaens, Katinka de Wet, Edwin Wouters

Community health worker (CHW) programmes are increasingly recognized as promising strategies to strengthen public health systems, improve access to care, and ultimately reduce health disparities, based on decades of experience in low- and middle-income countries. However, limited guidance exists on how to adapt these interventions to high-income settings, which requires understanding the mechanisms through which they operate and how these are shaped by context. This study examines South Africa’s national CHW programme as a case of integrating CHWs into a formal health system at scale, to identify elements that may be considered when designing a CHW intervention in Belgium. We conducted a qualitative study combining data from 37 in-depth interviews with stakeholders, 10 days of field observations, and an analysis of relevant policy documents. Data were collected in Bloemfontein (Free State Province) and Cape Town (Western Cape Province), South Africa. Using thematic analysis, we developed a conceptual framework of five mechanisms through which stakeholders understood the CHW programme to operate: (i) community embeddedness, (ii) health system integration, (iii) intersectoral collaboration and community mobilization, (iv) multilevel adaptation to local needs, and (v) building trust and relationships. At its core is the interplay between community embeddedness and health system integration, which stakeholders saw as central to CHWs’ role in linking underserved populations to primary care, but which also required careful balancing in programme design to ensure CHWs were not pulled away from community-based work. Trust cut across all mechanisms, both enabling them and being shaped by how well they operated. This framework offers insights into the conditions under which CHWs can bridge the gap between communities and the formal health system. It may inform the design of CHW interventions in Belgium and other countries seeking to address health inequities.
author: Laura Vroonen
